query: Which material can be used for to improve the ductility and toughness of the HfZrTi high-entropy alloy (HEAs), and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small, controlled addition of niobium (Nb) into the HfZrTi high-entropy alloy will promote the formation of finely dispersed, coherent nano‐precipitates that refine the microstructure and activate additional deformation mechanisms, thereby enhancing ductility and toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase HfZrTi high-entropy alloy exhibiting limited plasticity and low fracture toughness.
generation.intervention: Alloy the HfZrTi matrix with a small concentration of Nb during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Standard room-temperature mechanical testing conditions typical for assessing ductility and toughness.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-scale, coherent Nb-induced precipitates and refined grain boundaries formed within the alloy.
generation.mechanism: The Nb addition is expected to encourage a nano-scale dispersion within the HfZrTi matrix. These coherent precipitates serve to pin dislocations and mitigate stress concentrations at grain boundaries, thereby activating additional deformation mechanisms and reducing crack propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in tensile ductility (evidenced by improved elongation) and toughness (as seen by higher fracture strain and resistance to crack initiation), compared to the baseline single-phase HfZrTi alloy.
generation.baseline: The as-designed single-phase HfZrTi HEA with limited ductility and toughness.
generation.boundary: The Nb addition must be optimized; too little may not form effective precipitates, while too much could lead to the formation of unwanted secondary brittle phases.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal concentration of Nb and the quantitative improvement in properties remain uncertain until experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HfZrTi alloys with varying Nb additions (e.g., 0, 2, 5, and 8 atomic percent). Subject the alloys to identical processing and perform detailed microstructural analyses (using TEM and SEM) to detect nano-precipitate formation and grain refinement. Subsequently, conduct room-temperature tensile and fracture toughness tests to compare ductility and toughness with the baseline alloy.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the inclusion of Nb does not lead to the formation of coherent nano-scale precipitates and/or if the measured ductility and toughness of the Nb-added alloys are not significantly improved over the baseline HfZrTi alloy, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering

Abstract A NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (HEA) has been successfully synthesized by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructure and mechanical properties of this alloy are investigated. It is observed that only two types of body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solutions are formed in the powders after ball milling for 40 h. However, a new face-centered cubic (FCC) precipitated phase is observed in the BCC matrix of bulk material consolidated by SPS. The FCC precipitated phase is identified as TiO, due to the introduction of O during the preparing process of HEA. The compressive yield strength, fracture strength, and total fracture strain of the consolidated bulk HEA are 2709 MPa, 3115 MPa, and 11.4%, respectively. The excellent mechanical properties can be attributed to solid solution strengthening and grain boundary strengthening of the fine-grained BCC matrix, as well as the precipitation strengthening owing to the formation of TiO particles. Keywords: refractory high entropy alloy, microstructure, mechanical properties
